title: A Tiny Swimming Robot Powered by Living Muscle
summary:
Scientists at MIT have built a tiny swimming robot that moves with living muscle instead of a motor. The robot is a thin, bendy gel frame about the size of a stick of gum, with two fins covered in muscle cells much thinner than a human hair. The cells were changed so they squeeze tight when light shines on them.

Shining light on one fin makes it flap and push the robot through the water. By picking which fin gets light, scientists can steer it and change its speed. In tests, it swam and turned through a simple underwater maze. At its fastest, it moved about four body lengths in one minute, much slower than an Olympic swimmer's 65.

“The robot's quite strong, given its size,” said study author Ritu Raman of MIT.

The study, published in Advanced Functional Materials, describes the first very thin, flat robot that moves with living muscle. Raman believes such soft robots could one day do gentle jobs in places too fragile for normal machines, because living tissue is soft and can heal itself.
why_it_matters: It shows kids how science can turn a tiny idea into a gentle helper for delicate jobs.
